Nous reviendrons dans la suite sur l'origine de cette merveilleuse conception de l'esprit humain. Nous devons pour l'instant nous borner à disséquer la machine et à en montrer le mystérieux agencement.

Partant d'un principe fixe et immuable : la constitution du tétragramme sacré, *iod hé vau hé*, le Tarot développe les combinaisons les plus diverses sans jamais s'écarter de sa base. C'est cette étonnante construction, affirmant en application l'universelle loi des analogies, que nous allons dévoiler.

Les développements qui vont suivre paraîtront peut-être arides à quelques-uns; qu'ils songent que c'est une clef presque infaillible de la science antique ou science occulte que nous donnons là, et alors ils comprendront qu'ils doivent eux-mêmes ouvrir la porte de l'arche sainte.

->ÉTUDE D'UNE COULEUR<-

Prenons un des paquets de 14 lames et analysons sa construction.

Ce paquet, pris dans son ensemble, correspond à une des couleurs de notre jeu de cartes. Les 4 paquets représentent respectivement des *bâtons* correspondant à nos trèfles, des *coupes* correspondant à nos cœurs, des *épées* correspondant à nos piques et des *deniers* correspondant à nos carreaux.

C'est un de ces paquets, par exemple celui de bâtons, que nous étudions en ce moment.

Ce paquet est formé de 4 figures : le roi, la dame, le cavalier, le valet, plus dix lames portant simplement des nombres.

L'as, le deux, le trois, le quatre, le cinq, le six, le sept, le huit, le neuf et le dix.

We will return later to the origin of this marvelous conception of the human mind. For the moment, we must limit ourselves to dissecting the machine and showing its mysterious arrangement.

Starting from a fixed and immutable principle: the constitution of the sacred <term>tetragrammaton</term> <gloss>four-letter name of God</gloss>, <term>iod hé vau hé</term> <gloss>Yod-He-Vav-He, the Hebrew name Yahweh</gloss>, the Tarot develops the most diverse combinations without ever departing from its base. It is this astonishing construction, affirming the universal law of analogies in its application, that we are going to reveal.

The developments that follow will perhaps seem dry to some; let them consider that this is an almost infallible key to ancient science or <term>occult science</term> <gloss>hidden knowledge</gloss> that we are providing here, and then they will understand that they must themselves open the door of the holy ark.

->STUDY OF A SUIT<-

Let us take one of the groups of 14 cards and analyze its construction.

This group, taken as a whole, corresponds to one of the suits of our deck of cards. The 4 groups represent respectively <term>bâtons</term> <gloss>wands or scepters</gloss> corresponding to our clubs, <term>coupes</term> <gloss>cups</gloss> corresponding to our hearts, <term>épées</term> <gloss>swords</gloss> corresponding to our spades, and <term>deniers</term> <gloss>coins or pentacles</gloss> corresponding to our diamonds.

It is one of these groups, for example that of wands, that we are studying right now.

This group is formed of 4 figures <note>court cards</note>: the king, the queen, the knight, the page <note>original: "valet"</note>, plus ten cards simply bearing numbers.

The ace, the two, the three, the four, the five, the six, the seven, the eight, the nine, and the ten.

### LES QUATRE FIGURES

Voyons d'abord les quatre figures.
Le roi représente l'actif, l'homme, le mâle.
La dame représente le passif, la femme, la femelle.
Le cavalier représente le neutre, l'adolescent.
Enfin le valet figure le 4ᵉ terme de cette série que nous pouvons écrire ainsi :

->Roi<-
->Dame + Valet<-
->Cavalier<-

Cette série n'est qu'une application de la loi générale *iod hé vau hé* que nous connaissons bien et les rapports sont faciles à établir :

->Roi<-
->ou<-
->*Iod*<-
->Dame | Valet<-
->ou | ou<-
->1ᵉʳ *Hé* | 2ᵉ *Hé*<-
->Cavalier<-
->ou<-
->*Vau*<-

Le Valet correspond donc au *second Hé*, c'est-à-dire qu'il n'est qu'un terme de transition ; mais transition entre quoi?

### THE FOUR FIGURES

Let us first see the four figures.
The King represents the active, the man, the male.
The Queen represents the passive, the woman, the female.
The Knight represents the neutral, the adolescent.
Finally, the Page <note>original: "valet"</note> represents the 4th term of this series, which we can write as follows:

->King<-
->Queen + Page<-
->Knight<-

This series is only an application of the general law <term>iod hé vau hé</term> that we know well, and the relationships are easy to establish:

->King<-
->or<-
->*Iod*<-
->Queen | Page<-
->or | or<-
->1st *Hé* | 2nd *Hé*<-
->Knight<-
->or<-
->*Vau*<-

The Page thus corresponds to the <term>second Hé</term>, which is to say he is only a term of transition; but transition between what?
Between the four figures and the ten following numbers.

LES DIX NOMBRES

Occupons-nous donc maintenant de ces nombres. Nous connaissons la *Loi* des nombres ou loi des séries que nous avons énoncée antérieurement en ces termes :

7 — etc.

Les dix lames ne sauraient échapper à cette loi et nous pouvons les ranger de suite en série.

La première série sera formée de l'As ou 1 figurant *l'actif*, du 2 figurant *le passif*, du 3 figurant *le neutre* et enfin du 4 figurant *la transition* d'une série à l'autre.

1, 2, 3, 4 correspondent donc aussi à *iod hé vau hé* et se formulent ainsi :

THE TEN NUMBERS

Let us now concern ourselves with these numbers. We know the Law of numbers or the law of series that we previously stated in these terms:

1 — 2. 3
4 — 5. 6
7 — etc.

The ten cards cannot escape this law and we can immediately arrange them in a series.

The first series will be formed of the Ace or 1 representing <term>the active</term>, the 2 representing <term>the passive</term>, the 3 representing <term>the neutral</term>, and finally the 4 representing <term>the transition</term> from one series to another.

1, 2, 3, 4 therefore also correspond to <term>iod hé vau hé</term> and are formulated as follows:

# Alleum <note>Garlic</note> Kuoblauch

<note>A hand-colored woodcut illustration of a garlic bulb with long, green, blade-like leaves.</note>

Alleum <note>Garlic</note> is a plant and is twofold. One is domestic, the other wild, which is called <term>scoridion</term> <gloss>wild garlic</gloss>. It is heating and drying in the third up to the fourth degree, and the wild sort is more so than the other. From this, spasms can easily arise, which makes it a poison, and this occurs in the following way: let the seed of garlic be taken and planted, and from the seed produced by that garlic, let it be planted again, and let this be done five times or more. Then the garlic produced later will be a poison; thus, garlic should be transplanted and not grown from seed. This is done commonly for the reason already stated, although gardeners may be ignorant of it. Item: garlic is beneficial for alopecia <note>hair loss</note>.

<summary>This page introduces garlic, distinguishing between domestic and wild varieties and detailing the dangers of repeatedly planting garlic from seed, while noting its use for hair loss.</summary>

And when, just as he had foreseen, there was a great abundance of olives, he charged whatever price he wanted to the many who sought to buy them, and thus he collected much money. By doing this, he showed those who mocked him that it is not that philosophy is empty, for it is easy for philosophers to gain wealth, but that the study of philosophy and the study of money cannot exist together. Therefore, having left behind the lesser study, he had chosen to devote himself to the worthier study, that of philosophy. It is said of him that one night, when he was being led out of his house by an old woman to observe the stars, he fell into a pit. The old woman said to him while he was complaining, "You, O Thales, who cannot see what is before your own feet, how then could you recognize what is in the heavens?" This Thales is said to have said, "I give thanks to fortune for these three things: first, that I am a man and not a beast; second, that I am a male and not a female; third, that I am a Greek and not a barbarian." Concerning this Thales, Augustine says in book eight of *The City of God*: "Two types of philosophers are handed down: the Italian and the Ionian." And thus Thales of Miletus was the prince of the Ionian kind. He scrutinized the natures of things in order to propagate them to his successors, and he shone forth most brightly because he committed his disputes to writing and was indeed most admirable, for having grasped the numbers of astrology, he was able to predict the eclipses of the sun and the moon. He thought that water was the beginning of things, and from this, all elements of the world exist, and he himself was born from it. Isidore, in the second book of the *Etymologies*, says this: "Thales of Miletus was the first among the Greeks to examine philosophy, whence he is one of those who were called sages. For before others, he examined the turnings of the heavens and the complete account of all natural things." These things are said to be his sayings, as Laertius writes in his book on the lives of the philosophers: "The most ancient of beings is God, for he is unbegotten. The most excellent of beings is the world, for it is the work of God. The greatest of beings is place, for it contains all things. The swiftest of beings is the intellect, for it runs everywhere. The most valid of beings is necessity, for it masters all. The most prudent of beings is time, for it discovers all."

Concerning the life of Thales: He was asked by someone if a man doing something unjust is hidden from the gods. He said, "Not even by thinking it." Asked if he had ever committed perjury, he said, "Perjury is worse than adultery." Asked what is difficult, he said, "To know oneself." Asked what is sweetest, he said, "To obtain what one desires." Asked what is the divine, he said, "That which has neither beginning nor end." Asked what is the heaviest thing to see in the world, he said, "A tyrant." Asked how one can bear misfortune, he said, "If he sees his enemies bearing it." Asked how one can live justly, he said, "If he does not do himself what he commands others to do." Asked what makes a person happy, he said, "He who is healthy in body, resourceful by nature, and docile." He taught that one should remember friends both present and absent, and not to decorate one's face, but to be good in one's thoughts. He preached, "Do not be idle, and do not be cruel. Receive from your children the same care that you have offered to your parents." Anaximander the philosopher was a student of this Thales. Thales died in the sixty-seventh year of his life. He flourished in the times of King Achaz of Judea. And it is to be noted that when Egypt was punished by Moses and Aaron with so many plagues for five years, some who feared that Egypt would perish went out, just as Tyrops, who entered Greece and founded Athens, Epidaurus, and Corinth.

translation.data: When they had come to the king, they were kindly received by him. Staying for twelve days with the king, he inquired of them about things he had disposed of in his heart, and especially about two things: namely, the knowledge of God and the government of the kingdom. When they had instructed him in the administration of the kingdom, they then disputed more fully about worshipping the one God, [emphasizing] that no creature is God. Hence it is that wherever a mention of the Trinity occurred to them, they either passed over it in silence or translated it enigmatically, lest they appear to have taught that three gods should be worshipped. Similarly, mentioning the incarnation of the Word, as in Isaiah, when they had said, "A child is born to us," and he had added his names, for those six names they translated "Angel of Great Counsel," lest they appear to have taught that a man was made God. Then they showed the king the scroll they had, and he could not stop admiring the thinness of the pages and the pagination, which could not be comprehended by the eyes, and how the golden letters appeared so legible against the whiteness of the pages. They were introduced into the king's house by the sea, which was secret for the deliberation of business, and individual cells were given to them for whatever seemed opportune to them for translating. And, observing the rite of their purifications and prayers each day, they would wash themselves in the sea for the Law. Furthermore, they translated until the ninth hour, then they passed to food and rest, and they completed the work in seventy-one days. Augustine says that it was miraculously done that one and the same edition was found without difference, and that they translated the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets in so many days. Jerome, however, seems to want to say that the translators conferred on the Sabbath of six days, forging one from them all. The work being completed, Demetrius gathered all the Jews who were in Alexandria and those more skilled from the province, and their translation was read before everyone and approved. Furthermore, it was brought to the king and replicated before him. When the interpreters asked of the king that authority be given so that it might remain immovable, he praised that he would do this if at last they collected those things so chastely that what was once judged would not be forced to be irritated. And he sent them back honored with gifts. He also sent gifts to Eleazar. To the temple, however, he sent a vessel adorned with inappreciable gems, whose thickness was half a cubit, yet the workmanship exceeded the material. This Ptolemy composed canons of the stars and wrote many books. He was also very skilled and most learned in the quadrivium. He made a description of the orb of the earth and found the number of stadia of the earth and the circles of the earth with wonderful subtlety and ingenuity. At that time, the Carthaginians defeated the Romans in a naval battle, having put Metellus to flight, and captured Marcus Regulus with five hundred noble Romans and killed three hundred thousand of them. It is argued: Aristotle in the text commits the fallacy of the consequent, because he argues from a total conditional with the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent. It must be said that it is possible to argue in conditionals in two ways. One way is in convertible terms, and thus one can argue indifferently from the position or destruction of the antecedent or the consequent, because in non-convertible terms, if one is posited, the other is posited, and if one is destroyed, the other is destroyed. And thus it is argued here, because having a power and proper operation and being separable from the body are convertible for the soul, and therefore it is permitted to argue from the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent. The other way is to argue in non-convertible terms, and thus it is necessary to argue from the position of the antecedent to the position of the consequent, or from the destruction of the consequent to the destruction of the antecedent.

It is argued: It seems that the example of the text is inconvenient, because if a spherical body were to touch a straight line according to indivisible points, then the line would be composed of indivisibles. For the understanding of the argument, it must be known that if a bronze sphere moves over some hard surface, then it will be necessary to touch such a surface with the bronze sphere according to points, because if it were to touch according to some small quantity, then the bronze sphere would not be a perfect sphere, because it would have some surface according to which it would touch the hard thing, and this is repugnant to a sphere. Second, it must be known that because between two hard bodies there is some medium, therefore it is necessary to imagine that the bronze sphere is placed upon the surface of water, and the water does not yield.

With these considered, it must be said to the arguments that there is a double touch, namely metaphorical or mathematical, and physical. It must be said, therefore, speaking mathematically, that a bronze sphere touches a surface according to minimal surfaces and not according to points. Nor does it follow if it touched according to points that a continuum would be composed of indivisibles, because those points that the spherical body touches are not in act but in potentiality; therefore, a line is not composed of them, because it is only composed of those things that are in act. And to the argument, it must be said that the minimal or inconsiderable straightness in a spherical body does not impede sphericity, and therefore even if there are inconsiderable surfaces in the body, this does not impede its sphericity or spherical figure.

It is asked: Whether the soul is separable from the body? I respond that taking the soul for the vegetative and sensitive soul, those souls that are immersed in matter cannot be separated from the body. But taking the soul for the rational soul, then it is separable from the body because it is a form capable of subsisting by itself, as is clear in the third book of this work, where he says that the soul is that which truly is.

It is argued: The soul depends on the body; therefore, it is not separable from the body. I respond that the rational soul is taken in two ways. In one way, regarding its coming-to-be, and thus it depends on the body because it cannot come-to-be except in the body; because if it were to come-to-be outside the body, then it would be a separate substance and not a soul. And although the soul is in the body, it can be separated from the body while retaining the individuation that it received from the body. In the other way, the rational soul is taken regarding its being, and thus it depends on the body in two ways. In one way, subjectively, and thus sensitive powers depend on the body, but not the powers of the rational soul, because the intellect is not subjected in any corporeal organ, but is immaterial, as is clear in the third book of this work. In the other way, it depends on the body objectively, because the body is its object; and thus the soul also depends on the body even regarding the intellect, because the intellect for the state of this life cannot understand the immaterial as an object; therefore, the intellect objectively depends on material things, and this impedes its separability, because the intellect, even when actually separated from the body, as is the angelic intellect, can understand the body not withstanding its separation.

<column-break/>

It seems, however, and Aristotle makes manifest what he previously presupposed, namely that some things are among the passions common to the soul and the body. He proves this in three ways. The first reason stands in this: that those passions are common to the soul and the body, because the body also suffers something, because if the body suffers something, then they are also in the body. For many are the passions of the soul in which the body also suffers something, such as anger, joy, gentleness, fear, etc., because in anger there occurs a boiling of blood around the heart, therefore those passions are common to the soul and body. The second reason: those passions are common to the soul and body which are diversified according to the disposition of the body according to diverse times. But sometimes it happens that with great passions occurring, a man does not become angry, and it also happens at another time that with a lesser passion occurring, a man is more perturbed. The disposition of the air therefore contributes to this, because sometimes a man is more angered, as Aristotle says in <term>Meteorology</term> <gloss>study of atmospheric phenomena</gloss>, that when a comet reigns, then there are many wars between princes. The third reason stands in this: those passions are of the soul and body which vary according to diverse complexions <note>the humoral balance of the body</note>, because the complexion looks to the body, but these passions are in men in diverse ways according to diverse complexions, because there are some so complexioned that from the smallest terrors or from no impending evils, they fear much, as the <term>melancholy</term> <gloss>those with an excess of black bile</gloss> fear danger from mere imagination. Others are so complexioned that with great fears impending, they fear nothing at all.

as are the choleric. Therefore, since fear is a passion of the soul, it is manifest that some passions are common to the body and the soul together.

**If, however, it is thus.**

He infers the conclusion principally intended, correlatively, namely this: since it was said that if passions are common to the soul and body, therefore they ought also to be defined through the soul and the body, because each thing must be defined just as it has being. Since, therefore, these passions have being in the body, therefore they must be defined through the body. And so, Aristotle, defining anger, says this: Anger is a certain movement of the body, or of a part, or of a power for the sake of something of this kind. And this definition has four causes. In this, indeed, that he says "movement," he touches the formal cause, because every passion of the appetite is a movement insofar as "movement" is taken for the exit of potentiality into act. For Eustathius defines passion thus in the third book of the <term>Ethics</term> <gloss>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</gloss>: Passion is a movement of the appetite under the imagination of good or evil. Therefore, "movement" in the definition of anger cannot signify a flowing form, but the act of the appetite, just as in other definitions of passions, because speaking formally, passion is an act or operation of the sensitive appetite itself made with bodily alteration. And because it happens with bodily alteration, therefore it is called a passion. We impose names from things more known to us, because since such movement or alteration is more known to us, therefore we impose names from such a passion. He places further in the definition of anger "of the body or of a part," where he touches the material cause, through which this movement or this operation occurs, which is the body. Then "or of a power" is placed, in which the efficient principle is touched, because the irascible power is the principle of this movement or passion. "For the sake of something of this kind" is added, where the final cause is touched, because it is for the sake of the appetite for revenge.

**And on account of this, therefore.**

He concludes from the things said, because it was already said that some passions are common to the soul and body, that it pertains to the physicist to determine concerning the soul, namely in order toward such passions, or concerning the soul, or at least concerning the soul having such passions. And the reason is, because as is clear in the second book of the <term>Physics</term> <gloss>Aristotle's Physics</gloss>, the physicist must determine forms insofar as they are in matter. But the soul, at least according to these passions, is said to be a form in matter; therefore...

**Differently, however.**

He places the difference between the dialectician and the physicist regarding definition. And he distinguishes a triple definition: because one is given through matter only, one through form only, and one through form and matter together. He gives examples in the text concerning anger and man. Regarding anger, the definition given through matter is: Anger is a boiling of blood...

<column-break/>

...around the heart. That given through form is: Anger is an appetite for revenge. That given through form and matter together is: Anger is a boiling of blood around the heart on account of the appetite for revenge. Similarly, a house has three definitions. The first, formal, is this: A house is a covering keeping us from winds, rains, and <term>caumata</term> <gloss>heats/scorching temperatures</gloss>. The material one is this: A house is that which is composed of wood and stones. The other is that which embraces both.

It is asked: In what category is anger? I respond that anger can be taken in multiple ways. In one way, as it signifies the principle from which it proceeds, and thus, because it proceeds from the appetitive power which inclines toward the desired thing, it is in the category of quality in the second species. But it is taken improperly thus, because it is manifest that the appetitive power is not a passion, since there are many passions in one power. And therefore, when anger is defined in this way, one must not take "appetite" there for the appetitive power, but for the act of desiring. Therefore, anger is taken in the second way properly, and thus it is from the category of action, because anger is nothing other than the act of the irascible power made with bodily alteration, namely with the movement of blood to the heart. In the third way, anger is taken regarding the movement occurring in the body, and then it is taken improperly again, and thus anger is in the category of <term>ubi</term> <gloss>place</gloss>, because in anger a local movement of blood occurs from the exterior members to the heart.

**Which, therefore, is natural.**

He shows that that is physical. And he intends that that which is given through matter is physical but imperfect. But that given through form and matter together is physical and perfect. But that given through form only is logical. And the reason is that the physicist considers forms insofar as they are in matter, because thus it belongs to mobile things. Since, therefore, each thing must be defined just as it has being, therefore it is necessary for all physical things to be defined through matter. That the definition given only through matter is imperfect is clear, because cognition properly cannot be taken through matter unless form is added to it for that thing, for then the thing can be properly cognized. But because the logician abstracts from matter and from movement, therefore he defines through form alone.

It is argued: Matter cannot by itself signify you; therefore, there is no definition given through matter alone, because matter is a being in pure potentiality, but each thing is known insofar as it is in act. I respond that matter is twofold, namely, primary matter, which is the subject of substantial form, and from such matter, insofar as it is of this kind, cognition of a thing cannot occur unless it is taken with form or under form. The other is secondary matter, which is the subject of accidental form, and thus parts are the matter of whiteness, and from such matter a thing can be accidentally known, because matter taken in the first way is being in pure potentiality, but matter taken in the second way is being in act.

### But is there not some

He shows here the difference between the manual, the mathematician, and the metaphysician. And it differs in this way: the metaphysician considers forms insofar as they are separable from matter, and therefore defines them without any matter. But the mathematician and the manual laborer—who is a natural philosopher—define a form insofar as it is in matter. They differ, however, in that the mathematician considers forms insofar as they are defined by imaginable matter, but the natural philosopher and the manual laborer insofar as they are defined by sensible matter. But they differ, because the natural philosopher considers forms whose principle is nature, but the manual laborer considers forms whose principle is art.

### It is necessary to return

Aristotle refers to the intended point, because he made a digression from the point. And he says it is necessary to return to connecting what was said before, because it was said that those passions which are fury, fear, desire, and so on, are not separable from physical matter as animals are, insofar as they are animals. And such forms do not possess themselves like a line or a plane, which can be understood without sensible matter. Then he continues the statements to be made. And he intends that these aforementioned passions also belong to the soul. Thus, therefore, in that book, the soul must be determined. And we ought to determine about the soul, then this method must be observed, namely that he first treats the opinions about the soul. And if in some things they spoke well, this is to be accepted as truth, but if they did not speak well about something, we should avoid that same thing.

### The principle of the question

After Aristotle prefaced the proem of this book, he sets forth the treatise. And he treats in this book about the soul according to the opinion of the ancients. In the second [part], he sets forth the truth. And first he shows that no philosophers had the way of investigating the nature of the soul. And he says that since an ensouled thing differs from an inanimate thing by motion and sensation, therefore some philosophers investigated the nature of the soul from motion, [and] some from sensation. Indeed, those philosophers who inquired about the nature of the soul from motion said fire is the soul, because fire moves the most, some [said] heat, some [said] fiery atoms. But those who inquired about the soul from sensation or cognition said the soul is composed of all things, and that it would know all things. Plato, however, specifically said the soul is composed of number, namely from unity, and this regarding the intellect, from the binary regarding science, from the ternary regarding opinion, and from the quaternary regarding sensation. And the reason

<column-break/>

for this is: he attributed intellect to the monad <note>original: "ydee vnitatf"</note> because intellect is the habit of principles. But he attributed science to the duality, because science proceeds from principles to a conclusion, which are two. And therefore in science there is duality, namely principles and conclusion. But he attributed opinion to the ternary, because opinion, although it is from principles to a conclusion, is not, however, from conformable principles just as science is, because in science both principles are necessary, but in opinion one proceeds from one thing opined and another feared. Then he attributed sensation to the quaternary, because sensation is a bodily power, but the first bodily figure is quadrangular, just as the first superficial figure is triangular. Some, however, proceeded in the knowledge of the soul from motion and sensation, and they said the soul is a number moving itself, that is, a cognition moving itself. For by number they understood cognition, because only intellectual things can number.

### Since however and

He touches upon the diversity of the philosophers themselves speaking about the soul regarding the principles of the soul. For some placed the principles of the soul to be bodily, and some spiritual. And they differed regarding the multitude, because some placed one principle and some many. Those who placed the soul to have a bodily principle are diversified, because some placed fire, which is the most subtle. And whatever would be noble would have the soul in itself because it would move iron. For some said air, like Diogenes. Some vapor. Some said the soul is something most noble and is continuously moved in the body just as the body is moved, and in this it is assimilated to the celestial bodies, and this was the opinion of Antiphon. Some, however, more crude, placed water to be the principle, of which opinion Hippus was. For some said blood is the soul, because the soul cannot be without blood, and of this opinion is Tricias the philosopher, because sensation appears most in the blood. It is clear, therefore, that such philosophers inquired about the nature of the soul from three things, namely from motion or cognition, or from motion and sensation and from cognition. Arguitur si anima est in qualibet parte essentia. ergo per virtutem etiam in animalibus presentia. que potentia sequitur per essentia. et tunc est vera potentia. essentia sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia. essentia sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia. et patitur ad partes corporis et non ad totum corpus sibi proportionatur. et tunc non est vera potentia sequitur essentia. Alio modo accipit essentia animae sequitur essentia. et hoc per alii sic dicunt. utique tota essentia ibi est tota potentia in radice et non in actu.

Arguitur si anima est in qualibet parte corporis tunc sequeretur quod idem esset movens et motum simul. et idem moveret et quiesceret. et una manus moveri potest alia quiescere. et anima movere sursum et ad totum corpus. et idem moveret contrariis motibus quod est inconveniens. Domine dupliciter. Primo quod non proprie moveat alia parte corporis mota. quod quis anima moveret moto toto corpore non est movere ad motione partis. quia anima non est proprie parte. Secundo concessio quia anima est ad motione partis. tunc dicit domine quod non est inconveniens unum et idem passum moveri et quiescere et moveri contrariis motibus et hoc si motu non est perfecte una et continua. Exempli extra posita. ut aliqui contingit existentes in navi quiescere cum se et in moveri per motus navis. Ita contingit aliqui existente in navi moveri contrariis motibus quod est cum navi descendere et per motum proprie ascendere contra motum navis. Sile domine ex anima existente in parte corporis et qua partes animalis sunt perfecte continue sic una pars potest moveri alia quiescere. et una pars potest moveri sursum alia vero vorsum.

Arguitur anima rationalis est indivisibilis vel indivisibilis quod vel est corpore extensiva vel non extensa. si est corpore extensive sic est divisibilis. si non extensa sic est indivisibilis. Domine quod duplex extensio. quod est extensio quantitativa sicut albedo extendit in pariete. et sic anima non est extensa in corpore quod tunc divideret ad divisionem corporis. Alia est extensio essentialiter informat qualibet parte animae et non oportet quod sit extensum dividatur ad divisionem corporis divisi.

Quod autem quibus.
Dicenter solvit prima questione prius motam quod fuit. An vegetativum. sensitivum. et intellectivum sint partes animae diverse vel una anima. Domine quod ista dicta est vegetativum. sensitivum. intellectivum et motuum duplex. Uno put invenitur in animalibus segregatim. et sic sunt diverse animae. Ad sic probat Aristoteles quod quando inveniuntur in

<column-break/>

universis tunc penes istas animas sumit differentia animalium. sed differentia sumitur ex forma substantiali. ergo in diversis animas que tunc possibile esset diversitas animas que inveniuntur in uno eodem. et sic non significat diversitas animas. quod tunc possibile esset diversitas animas. Unum per homine non sunt diverse animae. quia tunc in uno homine sint vegetativum. sensitivum. intellectivum et motuum.

Querit utrum anima vegetativa. sensitiva. in intellectiva sit una anima vel plures animae. Domine quod ista tria in uno numero sunt una anima numero sicut in homine. et hoc per tribus rationibus ducentibus ad impossibile et una ratione omnium. Prima ratio stat in hoc. si plures formae substantiales essent in uno subiecto et materia sequeretur quod unum ens in numero esset plura entia substantialia. sic sequela est impossibilis. quod implicat contradictionem. Sequela tunc perque forma substantialis aliquid est simpliciter ens cum ipsa dat simpliciter esse. Si anima est forma substantialis. quia sunt plures animae in uno homine sunt plura entia substantialia. Secunda ratio sumitur ex modo predicandi. et stat in hoc. si anima sensitiva et intellectiva diverse sint animae tunc ista propositio homo est animal vel esset falsa vel per accidens. quod utrumque est contra intentionem Aristotelis. Secundo posterio. Sequela perque quod predicatio quod fit per diversas formas vel est falsa si formae non sunt subordinate. ut album est dulce. ibi predicatur diverse formae non subordinate. vel si formae sunt subordinate et predicatio per accidens. ut lupicies est colorata. lupicies est in subiecto primo. Siter quod ista propositio homo est animal et diversis formis. et forma rationali et sensitiva non est esse in primo modo per se. Tercia ratio stat in hoc. quod si anima vegetativa. sensitiva. et intellectiva essent diversae animae in uno homine sequeretur quod operationes factas ab alia anima. si hoc est falsum. ergo sunt una anima. Maior patet. quia quando sunt simpliciter diversa unum non impedit alterum. Minor quod si operatio unum animae fit multum intellectiva tunc impedit operatio sensitiva. contingit etiam et intellectiva virtutem et multum intenta imaginatione impediri virtutem intellectivam. contingit etiam et intellectiva impediri operationes sensitivas. Ratio omnium stat in hoc. sic et hoc numerum altior et supior ad numerum inferiorem. ita est haec anima dignior ad minus digna. sed si per hoc numerum includit inferiorem. quod supior anima includit inferiorem. sic intellectiva includit sensitivam et sensitiva vegetativam. Maior patet. quia species rerum sumitur ex animabus. sicut ergo species rerum se habent ut numeri ita et animae. et hoc quod dicit infra.

Book Two

It is argued: if the soul is in every part by essence, then it is also present by power in animals, since power follows essence. And then it is a true power, the essence is proportioned to itself, and then it is not a true power. It suffers toward the parts of the body and not to the whole body proportioned to itself, and then it is not a true power that follows essence. In another way, one accepts the essence of the soul as following essence. And others say it thus: certainly the whole essence is there, the whole power is in the root and not in act.

It is argued: if the soul is in every part of the body, then it would follow that the same thing would be moving and moved at the same time, and the same thing would move and rest. And one hand can be moved while the other rests, and the soul can move upward and toward the whole body, and the same thing would move with contrary motions, which is inconvenient. I say this is answered in two ways. First, that it does not properly move while another part of the body is moved; that the soul would move with the whole body being moved is not moving according to the motion of a part, because the soul is not properly a part. Second, conceding that the soul is according to the motion of a part, then I say that it is not inconvenient for one and the same patient to be moved and to rest and to be moved with contrary motions, provided the motion is not perfectly one and continuous. Examples are provided externally, as happens to some existing in a ship resting with it and being moved through the motion of the ship. So it happens to someone existing in a ship to be moved by contrary motions, which is to descend with the ship and by one's own motion to ascend against the motion of the ship. Similarly, I say that from the soul existing in a part of the body, and since the parts of the animal are perfectly continuous, thus one part can be moved and the other rest, and one part can be moved upward and the other downward.

It is argued: the rational soul is indivisible, or it is indivisible, either it is extensive in the body or not extensive. If it is bodily extensive, then it is divisible; if not extensive, then it is indivisible. I say there is a twofold extension. One is quantitative extension, just as whiteness extends in a wall, and thus the soul is not extended in the body, for then it would be divided according to the division of the body. The other is essential extension; it informs every part of the soul, and it is not necessary that what is extended be divided according to the division of the divided body.

As to which [soul].
The speaker solves the first question raised earlier, which was: whether the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective are diverse parts of the soul or one soul. I say that this is said: the vegetative, sensitive, intellective, and the movement are twofold. One way, as they are found in animals separately, and thus they are diverse souls. And thus Aristotle proves that when they are found in 

<column-break/>

all, then the difference of animals is taken from these souls, but the difference is taken from the substantial form. Therefore, there are diverse souls, which would then make possible the diversity of souls that are found in one and the same. And thus, it does not signify a diversity of souls, for then a diversity of souls would be possible. In a human, there are not diverse souls, because then in one human there would be a vegetative, sensitive, intellective, and movement.

He asks whether the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective soul is one soul or several souls. I say that these three in one number are one soul in number, as in a human, and this is by three reasons leading to the impossible and one reason of all. The first reason stands in this: if several substantial forms were in one subject and matter, it would follow that one being in number would be several substantial beings. Such a consequence is impossible, for it implies a contradiction. The consequence then is that through a substantial form something is simply a being, since it gives simple being. If the soul is a substantial form, because there are several souls in one human, there are several substantial beings. The second reason is taken from the mode of predicating, and it stands in this: if the sensitive and intellective souls were diverse souls, then this proposition "a human is an animal" would either be false or accidental, both of which are against the intention of Aristotle. Second, posteriorly. The consequence follows that the predication made through diverse forms is either false if the forms are not subordinate, as "the white is sweet"—there, diverse forms not subordinate are predicated—or if the forms are subordinate, the predication is accidental, as "a fox is colored," the fox is in the subject primarily. I say that this proposition "a human is an animal" and [with] diverse forms, the rational and sensitive form, is not to be in the first mode per se. The third reason stands in this: that if the vegetative, sensitive, and intellective souls were diverse souls in one human, it would follow that operations done by one soul [would not be hindered by another]. If this is false, then they are one soul. The major is clear, because when they are simply diverse, one does not impede the other. The minor is that if the operation of one soul is done, much intellective, then it impedes the sensitive operation; it happens also that the intellective [impedes] the power, and with much intent imagination, the intellective power is impeded. It happens also that the intellective impedes sensitive operations. The reason of all stands in this: as this number is higher and superior to the lower number, so this soul is more worthy to the less worthy. But if by this the number includes the lower, because the superior soul includes the inferior, thus the intellective includes the sensitive, and the sensitive the vegetative. The major is clear, because the species of things are taken from souls; as therefore the species of things relate as numbers, so also the souls, and this is what he says below.

He posits the second argument when he says, etc. It is as follows: If the soul is moved by itself, it moves naturally; now, everything that moves naturally moves violently. But if it moves naturally, it rests violently. Therefore, the soul moves violently and rests, which is impossible. But that which moves violently and rests, as the motion of the soul and rest are voluntary. In this argument, however, there seems to be a doubt, namely, why that which is moved naturally should move violently; for the heavens move naturally, but not violently. To this it must be said that this proposition is false in truth, but true according to the supposition. For those men posited no body to be moved naturally except for the four elements, in which we see motion and rest happen violently, and the argument proceeds according to this. <meta>A red decorative initial Q starts the section.</meta> He posits the third argument when he says, etc., "clearly, moreover." It is as follows: They say that the soul moves, and from this, it moves the body. This motion they say it has from one of the elements. Therefore, it follows the motion of fire, or earth, or other elements. If, therefore, it participates in the motion of fire, it will move only upward; if [of] earth, downward. But this is false, because the soul moves to every part, and this argument proceeds from their supposition. <meta>A red decorative initial Q starts the section.</meta> He posits the fourth argument when he says, "Since, moreover, it seems," etc. It is as follows: You say the soul is moved from this, that it moves the body; therefore, it is reasonable to say that the body is moved by those motions by which the soul itself is moved, and conversely, it will be true to say that it moves by those motions by which the body is moved. But the body moves by change of place; therefore, the soul moves by change of place. But if for the soul to be moved it must change the body, it is fitting for it, if it were to exit, to re-enter the body; and since to enter the body is to vivify the body, it follows from this that dead animals would rise again according to nature, which is impossible. Against this argument, some object, saying that this—namely, that the soul is moved by the same motions by which it moves—is not true, because the soul is not moved except according to appetite and will, while the body [moves] by other motions. To this it must be said that to desire, to will, and the like are not motions of the soul, but operations; motion is an imperfect act, whereas operation is a perfect act. Nevertheless, that proposition is natural according to their positions, because they said the soul is not otherwise mobile except according to how it moves the body. But does it not follow...

<column-break/>

that inconvenient thing, that the bodies of animals would rise again if the soul is moved according to place? It must be said that some have said that the soul is mixed with the entire body and united according to a certain proportion, and that it is not separated unless that proportion is dissolved. Whence, as far as those [thinkers] are concerned, it does not follow; but as far as those who say the soul is in the body as in a place or in a vessel, and that it enters and departs, sometimes that inconvenience follows. <meta>A red decorative initial Q starts the section.</meta> He posits the fifth argument when he says, <meta>A red decorative initial A starts the section.</meta> "Moreover, it happens according to accident," etc. It is as follows: It is certain that of that which belongs to something in itself, it is not necessary that it belong to it according to something else, unless perhaps by accident. If, therefore, it is in the soul that it moves by itself and has it by its own nature, it is necessary that the soul be mobile by itself; therefore, it does not need to be moved through something else and by another. But we see that it is moved by sensibles in sensing, and by appetibles in desiring; therefore, the soul is not moved by itself. To this the Platonists object, saying that the soul is not moved by sensibles, but they meet the motion of the soul, in which the soul courses through them. But this is false, because as Aristotle proves, the <term>intellectus possibilis</term> <gloss>possible intellect</gloss> is reduced by them—namely, by the species of sensible things—into act, and therefore it is necessary that it be moved by them in this way. <meta>A red decorative initial S starts the section.</meta> He posits the sixth argument when he says, "But truly even if it moves," etc. It is as follows: If the soul moves itself, it is certain that it will move according to its own substance; but everything that moves departs or exits from that from which it is moved, just as if something is moved by quality, it exits and departs from the quality by which it is moved. If, therefore, the soul is moved by its substance and moves itself, as they say, it will depart and exit from its substance, and thus motion will be the cause of corruption for it, which is necessary for those who said that through motion it is assimilated to divine things and is immortal, as appears above. And this argument proceeds as far as they are concerned, because they did not distinguish between operation and motion; for operation does not make one depart but perfects the operator, but in motion, it is necessary that there be an exit. <meta>A red decorative initial Q starts the section.</meta> "Some, moreover, also move the soul," etc. Above, the philosopher posited arguments in general against those who posited the soul to be moved in itself. Sentiri sine sensu: si sensus est quaedam ratio, et proportio et potentia illius magnitudinis. Deinde cum dicit, manifestum est ex his praemissis concludit solum quadam modo quod posset quaeri. Et manifestum est ex praedictis propter quod excellentia sensibilium corrumpat organa sensuum, et in organis sentiendi ad hoc quod sentiat est quaedam ratio, et proportio, ut dictum est. Si ergo motus sensibilis fuerit fortior, hoc organum natum est pati: solvit proportio et corrumpit sensum, et consistit in quadam proportione organi, ut dictum est. Et sicut sicut cum aliquis forte percutit cordas, solvit symphonia et tonus in qua proportione consistit. Manifesta est etiam ex praedictis ratio alterius quaestionis propter quod plantae non sentiunt: cum in habeat quadam proportionem ad quaedam sensibilia, scilicet ad tangibilia. Manifestum est enim quod calefacit et infrigidat. Et igitur quaerendo non requirit ad sentiendum, non enim habet medietatem complexionis inter tangibilia quod nullus sensus esse potest. Et non habet se huiusmodi principium quod recipit species sine materia sensu: sed accidit eis pati cum materia, et est materiale transmutatione. Deinde cum dicit dubitabit aut aliquis, movet quadam modo circa passione a sensibilibus, quae ei dixerat quod plantae patiuntur a sensibilibus. Primo movet dubium utrum ab aliis sensibilibus aliquid possit pati quod non habet sensum, puta ab odore: quod non habet olfactum, a colore quod non habet visum, a sono quod non habet auditum, secundo ibi. Simul autem inducit duas rationes ad ostendendum quod non, quia prima talis est, quod proprium olfactibilis est facere relfatu: odor autem facit olfactibile, ergo si aliquid facit olfactum, et quod facit olfatum sive faceret et littera odor facit: propria igitur actio odoris in quo sequitur quod suscipies actione odoris in quantum odor: habet sensum olfactus quod ergo non habet sensum olfactus non potest pati ab odore, et eadem ratio videtur de aliis et non quorumcumque posse pati a sensibilibus: sed solum habentium sensum. Secundam rationem ponit, ibi. Manifestum est autem quod corpus primum ad concludendum, manifestum est per experimentum: quod lumen et tenebra et odor et sonum nullus effectus facit in corpora insensibilia: nisi

forte per accidens: inquantum corpora bruta huiusmodi qualitates aliquando agunt: sicut aer quando est tonitruum scindit lignum, lignum enim patitur non a sono per se loquendo: sed ab aere moto. Tertio ibi. Sed tangentia, ostendit aliter esse de qualitatibus tangentibus, et dicit quod tangibilia et humores, id est, pores faciunt quaedam effectum in sensibilibus, sed bene intelligendum est de saporibus: non inquantum tangibile, et quantum tactum. Si ei corpora insensibilia non paterent a qualitatibus sensibilibus non esset ponere a quo paterent et alterarent corpora inanimata, nam tangibilia sunt qualitates active et passive elementorum quas accidit universaliter alteratio in corporibus. Quarto ibi, ergo ne illa, ostendit etiam quod alia tangibilia sensibilia agunt in quaedam res inanimatas: sed non omnes dicit ergo ne illa, ostendit alia faciant aliquem effectum et olfatu in res inanimatas, quod dicit: sed tamen non omne corpus passivum est ab odore et sono: sicut omne corpus passivum est a calore et frigore. Sed ab istis sensibilibus pati possunt sola corpora indeterminata et quae non manent, ut aer et aqua quae sunt humida et non bene determinabilia termino proprio, et quod aer possit pati ab odore manifestum est quia aer fetet sicut aliquid patens ab odore, alia littera habet feret: quia scilicet media et aliis sensibilibus feret species ad sensum, sed huiusmodi diversitatis est: quia alitates tangibiles sunt causae aliorum sensibilium, et ideo habent plus de virtute activa: et possunt agere in quecumque corpora: sed alia sensibilia quae habent minus de virtute activa: non possunt agere nisi in corpora valde passibilia, et sic etiam ratio est de luce corporum caelestium quae alterant inferiora corpora. Qui toti ibi, quod est igitur, solvit rationem et positam: dicens: quia si aliquid patitur ab odore quod non odorat: quid est odorare nisi pati aliquid ab odore, et respondet quod odorare est sic pati ab odore et sentiat odore, et erat non sic patitur ut sentiat quia non habet potentiam sensitivam: sed sic patitur ut sit sensibilis inquantum est medium in sensu.

Then, when he says <note>a red paragraph mark follows</note> "it is manifest from these premises," he concludes only in a certain way what could be asked. And it is manifest from the aforesaid why the excellence of the sensibles corrupts the organs of the senses, and that in the organs of sensing there is, for the purpose of sensing, a certain ratio and proportion, as was said. If, therefore, the motion of the sensible were stronger, this organ is born to suffer, it dissolves the proportion and corrupts the sense, and it consists in a certain proportion of the organ, as was said. And just as when someone strikes the strings forcefully, it dissolves the symphony and the tone in which the proportion consists. The reason for another question is also manifest from the aforesaid, why plants do not sense, since they have a certain proportion to certain sensibles, namely to tangibles. For it is manifest that it heats and cools. And therefore, in seeking, it does not require for sensing, for it does not have the mean of complexion between tangibles, without which no sense can exist. And it does not have that kind of principle that receives species without matter in the sense, but it happens to them to suffer with matter, and it is material through transmutation.

Then, when he says "some will doubt," he moves in a certain way regarding passion from the sensibles, which he had told it that plants suffer from the sensibles. First, he moves the doubt whether anything can suffer from other sensibles that does not have a sense, for example from an odor, that which does not have smell; from a color, that which does not have sight; from a sound, that which does not have hearing. Second, at the point "simultaneously, however," he induces two reasons to show that it does not. Because the first is such, that it is proper to the odorous to cause olfaction; odor, however, makes the odorous, therefore if anything makes olfaction, and that which makes olfaction or would make, the odor makes; the proper action of odor is therefore that in which it follows that you will receive the action of odor insofar as it is odor; therefore it has the sense of smell; what therefore does not have the sense of smell cannot suffer from odor, and the same reason seems to hold for others, and that not just anything can suffer from sensibles, but only those having a sense.

He poses the second reason there: "It is manifest, however, that the body first..." To conclude, it is manifest through experiment that light and darkness and odor and sound do not cause any effect in insensible bodies, unless perhaps by accident, insofar as brute bodies sometimes act by means of these qualities, as air when there is thunder splits wood, for wood suffers not from sound speaking per se, but from the air moved.

Third, at the point "but the tangibles," he shows it to be otherwise regarding tangible qualities, and he says that tangibles and humors, that is, pores, make a certain effect in sensibles, but it must be well understood regarding flavors, not insofar as it is tangible, and insofar as it is touch. If insensible bodies did not suffer from sensible qualities, it would not be to posit from what they would suffer and alter inanimate bodies, for tangibles are the active and passive qualities of the elements, from which alteration happens universally in bodies. 

Fourth, at the point "therefore, lest those," he shows also that other tangible sensibles act on certain inanimate things, but not all; he says therefore "lest those," he shows others make some effect, and smell, on inanimate things, which he says, but yet not every body is passive from odor and sound, as every body is passive from heat and cold. But from these sensibles, only indeterminate bodies can suffer, and those which do not remain, like air and water which are humid and not well determinable by their own limit, and that air can suffer from odor is manifest because the air reeks as something suffering from odor—another letter has "carries," because namely the media and other sensibles carry the species to the sense—but of such diversity it is: because tangible qualities are the causes of other sensibles, and therefore they have more of active virtue, and they can act on whatever bodies; but other sensibles which have less of active virtue cannot act except on very passive bodies, and thus also the reason is regarding the light of celestial bodies which alter inferior bodies. 

"Who, therefore," where he is, he resolves the reason and the position, saying: because if anything suffers from odor that does not smell, what is to smell except to suffer something from odor? And he answers that to smell is thus to suffer from odor and to sense the odor, and it is not thus suffering so that it senses because it does not have a sensitive power, but it is thus suffering so that it is a sensible insofar as it is a medium in the sense.

# The Division of the Sphere According to Substance

The sphere is divided in two ways: according to substance and according to accident. According to substance, it is divided into ten spheres: the tenth sphere, which is called the first motion or <term>primum mobile</term> <gloss>first moved thing</gloss>; the ninth sphere, which is called the second mobile. However, the words of the author teach the contrary to these: into nine spheres, namely the ninth sphere which is called the first motion or <term>primum mobile</term>; the stellar sphere of the fixed stars, which is called the <term>firmamentum</term> <gloss>firmament</gloss>; and the seven spheres of the seven planets. Of these, some are larger and some smaller according to how much they approach or recede from the firmament. Hence, among them, the sphere of Saturn is the largest, while the sphere of the moon is the smallest, as is contained in the following figure.

# The Division of the Sphere According to Accident

According to accident, it is divided into the right sphere and the oblique sphere. Those are said to have a right sphere who dwell under the equinoctial, if anyone could dwell there. It is called "right" because neither of the poles is elevated more than the other for them, or because their horizon intersects the equinoctial and is intersected by it at right spherical angles.

# What is the form of the world?

The universal machine of the world is divided into two parts: the ethereal and the elemental region. The elemental, indeed, being constantly subject to alteration, is divided into four. For the Earth, as the center of the world, is placed in the middle of all things; around it is water; around the water is air; around the air is fire, pure and not turbid, reaching the sphere of the moon, as Aristotle says in his book of <term>meteorology</term> <gloss>study of atmospheric phenomena</gloss>, speaking thus: God, glorious and sublime, arranged them in this way. These are called the four elements, which in turn alter, corrupt, and regenerate themselves. Elements are those which are simple, and which cannot be divided into parts of diverse form. From their commixture, diverse species of generated things are made. Any three of these surround the Earth orbitally on all sides, except in so much as the dryness of the Earth resists the moisture of the water to protect the life of living beings. All things except the Earth are mobile, which, as the center of the world, by its own weight, equally fleeing the great motion of the extremes from all sides, possesses the middle of the round sphere. Around the elemental region, the ethereal region—lucid and existing immune from all variation in its immutable essence—proceeds in continuous circular motion. This is called the fifth essence <note>original: "quinta essentia"</note> by the philosophers. Its spheres are nine, as was treated in the previous page: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Fixed Stars, and the ultimate heaven. Each of the upper ones surrounds the lower. There are two motions for these. One is of the ultimate heaven, upon the two extremities of the axis—that is, the arctic and antarctic poles—returning from the east through the west to the east, which the equinoctial circle divides through the middle. There is also another motion of the lower spheres, which is oblique, opposite to this, upon their axes distant from the first by twenty-three degrees and thirty-three minutes. But the first motion snatches all other spheres with its impetuosity once within a day and a night around the Earth, although they struggle against it, as the ninth sphere in one hundred years by one degree and twenty-eight minutes roughly, snatching with it the eighth sphere and all the apogees of the planets except the moon according to longitude, and therefore it is called the <term>primum mobile</term> <gloss>first moved thing</gloss>; to which the author's words are contrary: this eighth sphere in one hundred years by one degree. This motion is divided through the middle by the zodiac, under which each planet has its own sphere in which it is carried by its own motion against the motion of the ultimate heaven, and in diverse spaces of time it moves itself, such as the ninth sphere in forty-nine thousand years. The eighth sphere, by its own motion of trepidation, in seven thousand years. Saturn in thirty years. Jupiter in twelve. Mars in two. Hence Augustine bids us to attend to conscience, not indeed to the fame of honor; for this can be deceived, but conscience never can. Again, those who seek the friendships of kings and the favors of princes cannot rightly rejoice in the pinnacle of the greatest dignities. For dignity, as Tully says, is an authority worthy of honest cultivation and virtue and honor; when it comes from elsewhere, it should not be called dignity, but the usurpation of dignity. Hence Boethius says, "Sometimes honor does not accrue to virtues from dignities, but rather honor accrues to dignity from virtue; for a dignity conferred upon the wicked not only makes them unworthy, but rather betrays and reveals them." It is added that those who follow the shadow of a queen [or king] mostly do not attain dignities by virtues, by vice, not by merit, but by price; not by election, but by flattery. We shall therefore deal with that nobility of the flesh, which is reputed to be more worthy, more acceptable, and more honorable than among common people, which some call political nobility. We shall therefore inquire first what that nobility of the flesh is, and finally when, by what, and by what kind of means it is acquired. Therefore, omitting much that could be brought up here, it is enough for us to embrace the opinion of Aristotle. For he wished in his rhetoric that nobility be the same thing as the virtue of lineage. From this, indeed, we call some noble who trace their origin from an honorable family. Lineage, indeed, is called honorable by that reason, because from antiquity, many distinguished and honored men have proceeded from that progeny. And to speak briefly, this political ingenuousness, which the common people call nobility, is believed to be nothing other than having proceeded from some ancient lineage and honorable ancestry, in which from antiquity very many emerged as distinguished and honored men, either by ruling or presiding, or by exercising other public and honest acts either by the command of a prince or by the assent of the people. Decumis se eo peruenisse castris: et ultra ad fluuium qui niger uocatur: per solitudines nigri pulueris eminentibus interdum uelut exustis cautibus loca inhabita bilia feruore: quamque hyberno tempore expertos. Qui proximos inhabitent ei faltus refertos elephantorum ferarumque et serpentium omni genere canarios appellari. Quippe uictum eius animalis promiscuum iis esse: et diuidua ferarum uiscera. Iunctam aethiopum gentem quos perorros uocant fatis constat. Iuba Ptolemaei pater: qui primus utrique mauritaniae studiorum claritate memorabilior etiamque regno familia prodidit de atlante: praeterque sibi herbam euphorbia noie ab inuentore medico tuo appellatam. Cuius lacteu succu miris laudibus celebrat in claritate uisus cotraque serpentes et uenena omnia: priuati dictato uolumine. Et fatis superque de atlante.

The distance to it is immense and uncertain. There were also the journals of Hanno, the Carthaginian leader, who, when Punic affairs were most flourishing, was ordered to explore the circumference of Africa. Many, including Greeks and our own writers, have followed his account. They have reported other fabulous things and cities founded there, of which neither any memory nor trace exists. 

While Scipio Aemilianus was conducting affairs in Africa, Polybius, the compiler of annals, having received a fleet from him for the sake of exploring that region, sailed around it and reported that from that mountain toward the west, there are forests full of wild beasts which Africa generates, extending to the river Anatis for 485,000 paces. From there to Lixus is 205,000 paces. Agrippa says that Lixus is 12,000 paces from the Gaditan Strait. Thence is a bay which is called Faguti. A town on the promontory of Mulelacha. The rivers Sububa and Falat. The port of Rutubis is 313,000 paces from Lixus. Thence is the promontory of Folis; the port of Rifardir. The Gaetuli, the Autoteles; the river Cofenum; the tribe of the Felatiti and the Masafi; the river Mafathat; the river Darat, in which crocodiles are produced. Then a bay of 616,000 paces. Mountains are included there with the promontory of Barce extending to the west, which is called the Promontory of the Furies. Afterward, the river Palfus, beyond which are the Perorsi Ethiopians, behind whom are the Porusii. The Gaetuli Daras join these in the interior, but on the coast are the Daratitae Ethiopians. The river Bambothus is swarming with crocodiles and hippopotamuses. From there, continuous mountains lead up to that which we will call Eonochema. From there, a navigation of ten days and nights leads to the Hesperian promontory. In the middle of this space, he placed Atlas, reported by all others to be in the furthest reaches of Mauritania. 

Roman arms first fought in Mauritania under the Emperor Claudius. After King Ptolemy was killed by Gaius Caesar, his freedman Aedemon sought revenge, and it is agreed that when the barbarians fled, they came to Mount Atlas. It was a matter of glory, not only for those who had completed a consulship and held leadership in the Senate at that time, but also for the Roman knights who commanded there, to have penetrated to Atlas. As we have said, there are five Roman colonies in that province, and it may seem passable to rumor. But this is mostly discovered by a very deceptive experiment, because one is too lazy to investigate the truth by its own merit, and one is not ashamed to lie out of a sense of ignorance; there is no easier slide into false belief than when a grave author exists for a false matter. And, indeed, I am less surprised that certain things remain undiscovered by men of the equestrian order. Now, truly, even with those entering the Senate from elsewhere, what luxury! Its most effective and greatest power is felt when, with ivory and cedar wood being sought out, all the cliffs of the Gaetuli are covered with murex and purple dyes. Nevertheless, the natives report that on the coast, 150,000 paces away, is the river Afana, which is salt from the intake of the sea but remarkable for its port, and soon a river which they call Fuut. From there to Dirin—for it is agreed in their language that this is the name for Atlas—is 200,000 paces, with the river whose name is Uior intervening. There, rumor says that traces of formerly inhabited soil exist, remnants of vineyards and palm groves. 

Suetonius Paulinus, whom we saw as consul, was the first of the Roman leaders to cross Atlas, and he reported that it is some thousands of paces in height, indeed that which others have said. The lowest roots are filled with dense and tall forests of a kind of tree unknown to us, of remarkable height with a smooth, polished sheen, and leaves similar to cypress, but beyond the heaviness of their scent, they are covered in a fine down, which, by added art, could be fashioned into garments like those made of silk. The summit is covered with snow even in summer. He reached it in ten days' march, and beyond it to a river which is called Niger, through solitudes of black dust where places are uninhabitable due to the heat, with crags standing out that look as if they have been burned, and which he also tested in the winter time. Those who inhabit the forests nearest to it, filled with elephants, wild beasts, and all kinds of snakes, are called Canarii. This is because the diet of that animal is shared with them, and the entrails of wild beasts are divided among them. It is agreed by the Fates that the tribe of Ethiopians whom they call the Perorsi is joined to them. Juba, the father of Ptolemy—who was more memorable for the brilliance of his studies than for his kingdom, and even for his royal lineage—reported about Atlas, and furthermore, he discovered for himself an herb named Euphorbia, named after his own physician. He celebrates its milky juice with wonderful praises for its clarity of vision and its effects against snakes and all poisons, in a volume written for that private purpose. And enough and more than enough about Atlas.

Tingitania Province. Chapter 2.

The province of Tingitania is 170,000 paces long, and in it was the tribe formerly most prominent among the Moors, from whom the name of the province comes; most have called them the Maurusii. Weakened by wars, it has been reduced to a few families. Nearest to it had been that of the Massefyli, but it has just recently become extinct. Now the Getae hold the region: the Bamurae, and the Autololes, who are much more powerful. The province itself is mountainous from the east and produces elephants. In the mountain of Abila, also—which some call the Seven Brothers because of their similar height—and joined to Abila by the strait hanging over the sea, are the shores of the inner sea. The river Tamuda, formerly navigable, and a town. The river Laud, itself also capable of navigation. The town of Rufaddir and the port of Maluana. The river Figa is navigable. A town is situated opposite Maluana in Spain. It was the royal seat of Syphax, belonging to the other Mauritania. Indeed, the names of the kings held sway for a long time, so that the furthest part was called Bogudiana. Likewise the lands of Bocchus, which are now called Caesariensis. From there is the Great Port, called Harpatio, a town of Roman citizens. The river Mulucha is the boundary of the lands of Bocchus and the Massefyli. Quizacenitana is a town of foreigners. Arfennaria is a town of Latins, 3,000 paces from the sea. Carcenna is a colony of Augustus, established by the second legion. Likewise, a colony of the same [Emperor] was established with a praetorian cohort at Gunugi. The Promontory of Apollo. And a very famous town there, formerly called Caesarea—the royal seat of Juba—was granted the rights of a colony by the deified Claudius, with veterans settled there by his command. A new town was also established at Tipasa. Likewise, Icosium was granted the same gift by the Emperor Vespasian. The colony of Augustus at Rusguniae. Rufucurium was honored with the status of a city by Claudius. Rusasus is a colony of Augustus. Saldae is a colony of the same; the town of Gigili. Tucca is situated on the sea and the river Ampsaga. Inland is the colony of Augusta, which is also called Fuchabarita, Tubi, Subtu. Cities: Tirmici, Tigaua. Rivers: Ifarges, Gefnabades, Fardana, Lauerna, Bargenfina, Turebi, and the river Ufariens, which is navigable. The river Ampsaga is 233,000 paces from Caesarea. The length of both Mauritanias is 800,000 paces; the width is 339,000 paces. 

Numidia. Chapter 3.

Beyond the Ampsaga is Numidia, famous for the name of Masinissa, called the land of Metagonitis by the Greeks. The Numidians, however, are called Nomads because of their changing of their tents—their <term>mapalia</term> <gloss>huts</gloss>—which they carry around on wagons. Towns: Cullurus, Ichada. Forty-eight thousand paces from there, in the interior, is the colony of Cirtha, with the surname of the Sitiani. And another one inland, Sicca. And the free town of Bulla Regia. And on the coast, Tacatua and Hippo Regius. The river Armua. The town of Tachabracha, belonging to Roman citizens. The river Tusca is the boundary of Numidia. It has nothing else notable except for Numidian marble and its production of wild beasts.

Africa. Chapter 4.

Beyond the Tusca is the region of Zeugitana, and that which is properly called Africa. Three promontories: Candidum, soon that of Apollo opposite Sardinia; that of Mercury opposite Sicily, running into the deep sea, creates two bays. Hippone is nearest to the town which they call Hippo, destroyed, and Diarrhytus, called so by the Greeks on account of the irrigation of water. Neighboring it is the free town of Theudalis, further from the shore. Then the Promontory of Apollo; and in the other bay, Utica, a city of Roman citizens, noble for the death of Cato. The river Bagrada. The place of the Cornelian Camps. The colony of Carthage the Great on the ruins of Carthage; the colony of Maxulla. The towns of Carpi, Misua. And the Libyphoenices, who inhabit Bizantium—the region is so named—call it Clupea. It produces 250,000 paces in circuit of exceptional fertility, with the land returning a hundredfold harvest as interest to the farmers. Here are the free towns: Leptis, Adrumetum, Ruspina, Thapsus. Thence Thena, Auefinaco, Madefta, Chape, bordering the Lesser Syrtis, to which the length of Numidia and Africa from the Ampsaga is 580,000 paces. The width, as far as it is known, is 200,000 paces. That part which we have called Africa is divided into two provinces, the Old and the New, separated by a trench. It is led all the way to Thena, between the African follower and the kings; this town is 217,000 paces from Carthage. The third bay is divided into twin lesser syrtes by a shallow and ebbing sea. It is distant 300,000 paces from Carthage to the nearest, which is the lesser one.
