Polybius reports. It is 100,000 paces to the entrance, and 300,000 paces in circumference. And this land is noble for its faith or observation. The journey to it is through deserts of sand and snakes. Forests filled with a multitude of wild beasts receive travelers, and further inside are solitudes of elephants, soon after vast deserts. On both sides are the Garamantes, distant by a twelve-day journey from the Augilae. Above them were the tribe of the Psylli; above them, the Lake of Lycomedes, surrounded by deserts. The Augilae themselves are located in about the middle distance from Ethiopia, which inclines toward the west, and from the region which lies between the two syrtes, with an equal interval on both sides, but the coast between the two syrtes is 250,000 paces. There is the city of Oensis. The river and region of Cyniphos. The towns of Neapolis, Taphra, Habrothonum. Another Leptis, which is nicknamed Magna. The Greater Syrtis is 125,000 paces in circumference, and 313,000 paces at the entrance. Thence the tribe of the Cifipades dwells. In the bottom of the bay was the coast of the Lotophagi, whom some called Alachroae, at the Altars of the Philaeni, which are made of sand. Not far from these on the continent is a vast marsh to the river Triton. And it received its name from it, called Palatias by Callimachus, and said to be on this side of the lesser syrtis, but by many, between the two syrtes. The promontory which encloses the greater one is called Burion; beyond it is the Cyrenaica province. To this end, Africa from the river Ampsaga has twenty-six peoples who obey the Roman Empire. Among them are six colonies, beyond those already mentioned above: Uthina, Tuburbum. Fifteen towns of Roman citizens, of which must be mentioned in the interior: Absuritanum, Abutuncense, Aborienta Canophicum, Chimanense, Rhimituenfe, Thunufidiense, Tuburbiense, Tybidrumense, Tibigense. Two Ucitanae, greater and lesser. Uagense. One Latin town, Uzzalitanum. One tributary town. In the Cornelian Camps, thirty free towns, of which must be mentioned inland: Acolitanum, Acharitanum, Auinense, Abziritanum, Canopitanum, Melzitanum, Mararenfe, Salaphitanu, Tusdritanum, Diricense, Thiphicefe, Tunifese, Schoedenfe, Tagafenfe, Figenfe, Ulufuburitanu, another Uagense, Figenfe, Zianiese. From the remaining number, not only cities, but most nations can also be called by right, such as the Nattabudes, Capitani, Mufulani, Sabarbares, Massyllini citizens, Uamacures, Ethini, Muffini, Marchubi, and the whole of Gaetulia to the river Niger, which separates Africa from Ethiopia. Chapter 5.

Cyrenaica, the same as the Pentapolitan region, is illuminated by the oracle of Hammon, which is 400,000 paces from Cyrene at the Fountain of the Sun; the Pentapolis is named for its five cities: Berenice, Arsinoe, Ptolemais, Apollonia, and Cyrene itself. Berenice is in the furthest corner of the syrtes, formerly called that of the Hesperides in the wandering fables of Greece. And not far before the town is the river Lethon and a sacred grove, where the gardens of the Hesperides are mentioned. It is 385,000 paces from Leptis. From it, Arsinoe, called Theutyra, is 43,000 paces. And then Ptolemais, by the ancient name of Barce, is 22,000 paces. Soon 250,000 paces to the promontory of Phycus, which runs out through the Cretan sea, distant 350,000 paces from the promontory of Taenarus in Laconia, but 125,000 paces from Crete itself. After that, Cyrene is 11,000 paces from the sea. From Phicunte to Apollonia is 24,000 paces; to Chersonesus, 88,000 paces. From whence to Catabathmus is 216,000 paces. The Marmaridae inhabit from about the region of Pharedon as far as the Greater Syrtis. After them are the Acrucae and Lefatiani. On the coast of the syrtis are the Nasamones, whom the Greeks previously called Mesamones from the argument of the place, situated in the middle between the sands. The Cyrenaic field is considered fertile with trees for a width of 15,000 paces from the shore. Inland for the same space, only with crops, soon for a width of 30,000 paces, and for a length of 250,000 paces, [it is fertile] only in laserpitium. After the Nasamones, the Hasbytae and Macae live. Beyond them are the Hammanientes, an eleven-day journey from the Greater Syrtes to the west, and they themselves are surrounded by sands on every side, yet they find wells not difficult, about two cubits in height, with the waters of Mauritania stagnating there. They build houses from salt and mountains cut out like stone. From them to the Troglodytae is a journey of four days toward the region of the winter sunset, with whom the commerce is only in a gem, which we call a carbuncle, carried from Ethiopia. Intervening to the solitudes of Africa above the Lesser Syrtis is Verphazania, where we subdued the tribe of the Phazanii and the cities of Alelen and Cillaba. Ad isededu decoctum i duritia uuluarum: & i inflammationibus. Siccatum cum melle & aceto impositum bile detrahit atra. Ob hoc contra uertigines utilis. Et calculosis. Illinitur & sacro igni. Item strumis cum axungia ueterata. Magi contra tertianas sinistra manu euelli ea iubent: dicique cuius e ea uellat: nec respicere. dein eius folium agri lingua subicere: ut mox in cyatho aquae deuoretur. 
DE Strychne medicinae. Cap. xxxi.

s Trychne qua qua strychnum scripsere: utinam nec coronari i aegypto uteret: quos i uitat hederae foliorum similitudo: i duobus eius generibus: quorum alteri cui acini coccinei: granosi folliculi. Halicaccabum uocat & halicallion: nostri autem uesicaria: quoniam ueruecinae & calculis prodest: frutex est furculosus ueriusque herba: folliculis magnis: latisque & turbinatis: gradi itus acino q mateficit nouebri mese. Tertio folia sunt ocimi minie diligenter demonstranda. remedia. n. non uena tractatus: quppe insania facit puo quoque fucco: que & graeci auctores i iocu uertere. Drachmae. n. podere pudoris gigni dixerunt: spes uanas imaginesque conspicuas obseruari demonstrantes. Duplicatum huc modu: legiti ma insania facere. Quicquid uero adiciat podere repraesentari morte. ab eo que cuspides i praeliis tigeret illo: passi nascete: quo ptius spectabat. Magi cognouere que neqter occultabant: erythro: aut neurita: ut nonnulli pisone cauedi eqde ca curiosius didu. qn & altu genus q halicacabo uocat: soporiferum est: atque et opio uelocius ad morte: ab aliis morio: ab aliis moly appellatum. Laudatu uero a locro ad fruedu & timaristo: qda et carmie miore obliuione educetes. qppe praefetaneu remediu ad detiu mobiles firmados si collueret. Halicacabo uni exceptione addidere ne diutius id fieret. Deliratione. n. gigni eo. Nec demonstrada remedia: quorum medicia maioris mali piculu afferat. Comedat. n. cibis ttiu: licet praferat hortelis faporibus. Et nihil fit corpis malor: cui no salutare fit strychnos Xenocrates praedicet. Of <term>anthalium</term>, which the Egyptians eat, I have found no other use. And this is an herb. <term>Antillium</term>, which others call <term>aticellium</term>, is of two kinds: the first is similar to a lentil in leaves and branches, a palm in height, growing in sunny, legendary places, tasting somewhat salty. The other has leaves shorter and hairier than the germander, with a purple flower and a heavy scent, growing in rocky places. The former is most suitable for the womb. And when applied with rose-oil and milk, it is good for wounds. It is drunk for strangury and kidney pains in the amount of three drachms. The other is drunk for hardness of the womb, for colic, and for epilepsy with honey and vinegar in the amount of four drachms.

OF MEDICINES FROM <term>PARTHENIUM</term>. CHAPTER XXX.

Some call <term>parthenium</term> <gloss>feverfew</gloss> by the name <term>leucanthemum</term>, others <term>thanacum</term>. Celsus, in our language, calls it <term>pellecium</term> and <term>muralium</term>. It grows in gardens and hedges, with a white flower, an apple-like scent, and a bitter taste. It is used as a decoction for hardness of the womb and for inflammations. Dried and applied with honey and vinegar, it draws out black bile. For this reason, it is useful against dizziness and for those with kidney stones. It is also applied to holy fire <gloss>erysipelas</gloss>. Likewise for scrofula when mixed with old lard. Magicians order that it be plucked with the left hand against tertian fevers, that one should say whose name it is being plucked for, and that one should not look back. Then, they place a leaf of it under the tongue of the patient so that it may soon be swallowed in a cup of water.

OF MEDICINES FROM <term>STRYCHNE</term>. CHAPTER XXXI.

Would that they did not use <term>strychne</term> <gloss>nightshade</gloss>—which some have written as <term>strychnum</term>—for wreaths in Egypt, as the similarity of its leaves to ivy misleads them. It has two kinds: one has scarlet berries in granular pods. They call it <term>halicaccabum</term> and <term>halicallion</term>; our people call it <term>vesicaria</term> <gloss>bladder-herb</gloss>, because it is beneficial for sheep and kidney stones. It is a branched shrub, or rather an herb, with large, wide, and conical pods; it is known by the berry which it produces in the month of November. The leaves of the third kind are like those of basil and must be demonstrated carefully. For these remedies are not to be taken lightly, since the juice alone induces insanity, which the Greek authors have even mentioned in jest. They say that a weight of a drachm induces a sense of shame, demonstrating that one observes vain hopes and conspicuous images. It doubles this way: it induces legitimate insanity. Truly, whatever is added to the weight results in death. This was used by those who touched the tips of their weapons in battle, so that they might be born anew, as they previously envisioned. The magicians knew things that they did not hide from others, such as <term>erythro</term> or <term>neurita</term>, as some, like Piso, have learned more carefully. For there is another kind, which they call <term>halicaccabum</term>, which is soporific and faster to death than opium; some call it <term>morio</term>, others <term>moly</term>. It was praised by Locrus to Euedus and Timaristos, who also used it in an ointment to induce forgetfulness, for it is a preferred remedy to calm those who are restless if they wash with it. To <term>halicaccabum</term> alone they added an exception: that it not be done for too long, as delirium is born from it. Nor should remedies be demonstrated whose medicine brings the danger of a greater evil. For it is eaten in foods, even if it is preferred for its garden-like flavors. And there is nothing among the evils of the body for which <term>strychnos</term> is not healthy, as Xenocrates proclaims. However, their aids are not so great that it would be considered a sacrilege not to mention them, especially given such an abundance of harmless medicines. They drink the root of <term>halicaccabum</term> when those who are skilled in prophecy wish to be seen as mad in order to confirm their predictions. It is a remedy; I would rather report it as having been given in copious warm honey-wine. Nor will I omit that it kills by the power of sleep. Therefore, crushed in oil, it helps those who have been struck.

OF <term>CORCORUS</term>. CHAPTER XXXII.

<term>Corcorus</term> <gloss>jew’s mallow</gloss> is an herb of the Alexandrians, with curled leaves similar to those of the mulberry. It is useful for the midriff, and for hair loss and lichen <gloss>a skin condition</gloss>. It is also used to treat the mange of cattle very quickly, according to Nicander, and it is used for the bites of serpents before they flower. Nor shall I argue at length about <term>cnicus</term> or <term>atractylis</term>. It is an Egyptian herb and provides great aid against venomous animals. Likewise against fungi. It is agreed that those struck by a scorpion do not feel the torture as long as they hold that herb. 

OF <term>PFOLUTA</term>. CHAPTER XXXIII.

Egypt sows <term>pfoluta</term> in gardens for wreaths; there are two kinds: female and male. Both are highly reported to inhibit men's desire when taken. 

OF MEASURES AND WEIGHTS. CHAPTER XXXIV.

And since one must frequently use Greek terms for measures and weights, I will place their interpretation here once. The Attic drachma—for doctors use the Attic observation—has the weight of a silver denarius. It makes six obols in weight. An obol is ten chalchi. A cyathus weighs ten drachms by itself. When the measure of an acetabulum is spoken of, it signifies a fourth part of a hemina, that is, fifteen drachms. What our people call a mina weighs one hundred Attic drachms.
